title: Senior Living Research Digest — October 2026
secondary_audience: families, caregivers, and senior living professionals

studies.title: Sleeping pills stopped in the hospital often come right back home with you
studies.the_study: French researchers reviewed records for 155 patients aged 75 and older who arrived at an acute geriatric ward already taking benzodiazepines or related sleep/anxiety drugs (often called 'Z-drugs'). Doctors started reducing or stopping these medications in 61% of patients during the hospital stay, but among the 79 patients with follow-up prescription data, roughly one in four (26.6%) had their dose climb back up within 12 months of discharge. The only factor clearly linked to that rebound was managing one's own medications at home (odds ratio 4.86).
studies.why_it_matters: Benzodiazepines are tied to falls, fractures, confusion and daytime sedation in older adults, and this shows the hard-won reduction achieved in the hospital frequently unravels once someone gets home without a clear follow-up plan.
studies.story_angle_primary: If a sedative or sleeping pill was lowered or stopped while you were in the hospital, treat the discharge paperwork as the start, not the end: ask who is monitoring the taper, what withdrawal or rebound insomnia might feel like, and schedule a check-in with your regular prescriber or pharmacist within a few weeks so the dose doesn't quietly creep back.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For families and care teams, the care transition itself is the weak link — consider reconciling medications after discharge, flagging a stopped benzodiazepine to the primary care physician and community pharmacist, and recognizing that independent medication self-management, while valuable, may need extra support in the months after a deprescribing attempt.
studies.caveats: Single-center, retrospective and observational — it cannot establish cause; follow-up prescription data were available for only 79 patients, and the authors describe the analysis as exploratory with wide confidence intervals requiring confirmation in larger prospective studies.

studies.title: How long does Medicaid home care actually last? A decade of data offers an answer
studies.the_study: Researchers linked Southern Community Cohort Study data to Medicaid and Medicare claims to follow 1,304 older adults in Southeastern states who started Medicaid-funded home- and community-based services (HCBS) between 2006 and 2018. Among the 591 followed for five years, 32.3% were still receiving home-based services, 25.2% had stopped while remaining in the community, 16.2% moved to a nursing home and 26.2% had died. Older age, more health conditions and prior nursing home use predicted faster cessation, while women stayed on services longer.
studies.why_it_matters: Home- and community-based services are the main alternative to nursing home placement, and these numbers show most older adults who start them use them for years — useful context for anyone planning long-term care finances or weighing whether staying home is realistic.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you are considering Medicaid-funded home care, know that long enrollments are the norm rather than the exception, and that only about one in six people in this study ended up transitioning to a nursing home over five years — worth discussing with a benefits counselor or your state's aging and disability resource center when you map out your long-term plan.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For senior living operators and policymakers, the finding that a third of beneficiaries were still enrolled after five years speaks to budget sustainability and workforce planning: projections that assume short, episodic home care use may badly underestimate demand, and the pathway into nursing homes is narrower than often assumed.
studies.caveats: Observational claims-based analysis — cannot establish causation; limited to Southeastern states and a single cohort, so results may not generalize nationally; data predate recent Medicaid policy changes; the five-year subgroup was 591 people.

studies.title: Spinal fluid tests show Alzheimer's-type damage hiding inside Lewy body dementia
studies.the_study: An international consortium measured four cerebrospinal fluid markers — amyloid beta 42/40, p-tau181, neurofilament light and total alpha-synuclein — in 347 participants spanning Alzheimer's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), Parkinson's disease and healthy controls, all using the same automated assays. People with DLB frequently showed abnormal amyloid and tau levels, and those with that added Alzheimer's pathology had worse global cognition, though not worse motor function. Parkinson's patients largely did not show the Alzheimer's signature, while neurofilament light was elevated across all the diseases.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests that a substantial share of people diagnosed with Lewy body dementia also carry Alzheimer's pathology that is dragging their thinking down — information that may shape prognosis conversations and eligibility for amyloid-targeting treatments and trials.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you or a loved one has been diagnosed with dementia with Lewy bodies, it is reasonable to ask the specialist whether biomarker testing (spinal fluid or an equivalent) would clarify whether Alzheimer's pathology is also present, since that can affect what to expect and which clinical trials you might qualify for.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For care professionals, the message is that 'Lewy body dementia' is not one uniform trajectory: mixed pathology is common and tracks with faster cognitive decline rather than motor decline, which has implications for staffing cognitive support versus mobility support in individualized care plans.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional comparison in a research cohort of 347 — not a general-population sample; several authors report extensive industry ties and one is a Roche Diagnostics employee (Elecsys assays are Roche products), with Sanofi affiliation also represented; findings describe associations, not treatment effects.

studies.title: A curled toe can rob you of nearly 60% of your push-off power when you walk
studies.the_study: Researchers used 3D motion capture and force plates to compare walking in 17 adults with clinically diagnosed hammertoe deformity (28 limbs) against 30 age-matched healthy controls. Those with hammertoes generated 58.7% less ankle push-off power and 41% lower braking and propulsive forces, with reduced knee and hip range of motion and increased hip power during weight acceptance — a sign the body shifts work from the foot and ankle up to the hip.
studies.why_it_matters: Weak push-off and reduced propulsion are hallmarks of slower, less stable walking in later life, so a common and often-dismissed foot deformity may be quietly undermining mobility and the reserve that protects against falls.
studies.story_angle_primary: If your toes have begun to bend or claw and you've noticed your walk feels slower or more effortful, don't write it off as cosmetic — bring it up with a podiatrist or your physician, and ask whether footwear changes, toe spacers, stretching or strengthening could help preserve your push-off.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For caregivers and senior living staff, this is an argument for routine foot inspection as part of mobility and fall-risk assessment; a resident whose gait has subtly changed may have a treatable forefoot problem rather than generalized frailty.
studies.caveats: Small sample (17 patients) and cross-sectional, so it cannot show that hammertoes cause mobility decline or falls; single-center laboratory study; participant ages are not specified in the abstract beyond age-matching, so applicability to the oldest adults is uncertain.

studies.title: A routine cholesterol number may predict whether ED pills will work for you
studies.the_study: Turkish urologists followed 134 men aged 40 and older starting daily 5 mg tadalafil for erectile dysfunction over 12 weeks, calculating each man's atherogenic index of plasma (AIP) — a ratio derived from standard triglyceride and HDL cholesterol results. Overall, 73.1% responded meaningfully, but non-responders had higher baseline AIP, higher BMI and more than double the rate of diabetes; each 0.1-unit rise in AIP raised the odds of non-response by about 20%, and diabetes tripled those odds.
studies.why_it_matters: Erectile dysfunction in older men is frequently an early signal of vascular and metabolic disease, and this reinforces that lipid and blood sugar problems not only accompany ED but may blunt the response to standard treatment.
studies.story_angle_primary: If a daily ED medication isn't working as well as you hoped, it's worth asking your doctor to review your triglycerides, HDL cholesterol and blood sugar — the same metabolic picture that drives heart disease may be part of the reason, and addressing it is good for far more than your sex life.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For clinicians and care teams, poor response to a PDE5 inhibitor can serve as a prompt for broader cardiometabolic screening in older men rather than simply escalating the dose.
studies.caveats: Single-center prospective cohort with no control group and only 12 weeks of follow-up; the predictive accuracy was modest (AUC 0.650), and the authors stress AIP is at best an adjunctive marker, not a decision tool; observational design cannot establish causation, and the Turkish single-site population may not generalize.

studies.title: A routine blood test may predict survival in people who reach 100
studies.the_study: Researchers followed 1,002 community-dwelling centenarians in Hainan, China, calculating a "sarcopenia index" (SI) from two standard blood values — serum creatinine divided by cystatin C, multiplied by 100 — and tracked deaths over several years. Each one-unit increase in the index was tied to a 3.7% lower death rate, with risk dropping sharply as the index rose before leveling off. Optimal cutoffs for predicting death were roughly 59 at one year, 63 at three years and 64 at five years, though the overall accuracy of the measure was only moderate.
studies.why_it_matters: Muscle health is a major driver of survival in very old age, but DXA scans and specialized testing are expensive and often unavailable in primary care; this index uses blood work many older adults already have done.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you're curious about your muscle health, know that researchers are exploring whether ordinary blood markers you may already have on file — creatinine and cystatin C — can flag muscle loss. It isn't a diagnostic test, so the more useful conversation with your doctor is about grip strength, walking speed, protein intake and resistance exercise, which remain the practical ways to protect muscle.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For clinicians and senior living health teams in resource-limited settings, this points toward a low-cost way to triage who needs closer attention — but the authors are explicit that it's a surrogate marker with moderate discrimination, not a replacement for functional assessment.
studies.caveats: Observational cohort — cannot establish causation; single region of China in an extremely old, possibly unrepresentative population; the index is a surrogate, not a direct measure of sarcopenia, and its predictive accuracy was only moderate.

studies.title: Bed alarms don't prevent falls in hospitals — and experts are now trying to phase them out
studies.the_study: A review team examined the evidence base for fall prevention alarms used in hospitals — the bed and chair sensors that sound when a patient tries to get up — alongside other fall prevention practices. They catalogued why alarms remain so widely used despite weak evidence of benefit, and surveyed strategies being tested to "de-implement" them, drawing on the science of reducing low-value care.
studies.why_it_matters: Alarms are nearly universal in hospitals and many care settings, yet they can increase noise, disrupt sleep, add to staff alarm fatigue and discourage patients from moving — while the evidence that they actually prevent falls is thin.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you or a loved one is hospitalized and a bed alarm is switched on, you're entitled to ask what it's for and whether it's helping. Ask instead about the things that do have support: a medication review, mobility assistance, toileting schedules and safe footwear — and be clear that you don't want to be discouraged from moving when it's safe to do so.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For nursing leadership and senior living administrators, this is a roadmap for a difficult culture change: alarms persist partly because removing them feels like abandoning safety. The review frames de-implementation as a measurable quality project rather than a retreat from fall prevention.
studies.caveats: This is a narrative review rather than new primary data; it does not report a trial of alarm removal, and the hospital focus may not translate directly to long-term care settings.

studies.title: Starting, stopping and turning reveal Parkinson's changes that plain walking misses
studies.the_study: Using the open-access WearGait-PD dataset, researchers analyzed motion-sensor data from 91 people with Parkinson's disease and 78 controls wearing small sensors on the lower back and both feet. Beyond steady walking, they examined gait initiation, turning and gait termination. While stride length and walking speed declined with disease severity during steady walking, additional measures — how high the foot lifted, swing time and foot contact angle — only showed meaningful links to severity during the complex tasks of starting, turning and stopping.
studies.why_it_matters: Clinical assessments often watch someone walk a straight hallway, which can look deceptively normal; the moments that most often precede falls at home are turning, starting up and coming to a stop.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you have Parkinson's disease, notice whether your hardest moments are turning in the kitchen, rising to start walking, or stopping at a door — and describe those specifically at your next appointment rather than just saying "my walking is worse." Physical therapy cues for turning and initiation exist precisely for these transitions.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For caregivers and senior living staff, this supports designing the environment around transitions: wider turning space at bed and toilet, clear floor at doorways, and grab points where someone has to start or stop moving.
studies.caveats: Observational, laboratory-based cross-sectional analysis of an existing dataset — no causal or predictive claims about actual falls; lab tasks may not reflect real-world home mobility; no longitudinal follow-up.

studies.title: Personalized brain stimulation for stubborn depression fails to beat placebo in a controlled trial
studies.the_study: Fifty-one patients with treatment-resistant depression were randomized to one of three arms: accelerated intermittent theta burst stimulation (a rapid form of transcranial magnetic stimulation) targeted using individual brain MRI scans; the same plus EEG-based individualized stimulation frequency; or sham stimulation. Participants received 10 sessions a day for five consecutive days, with assessments at one and four weeks. Neither personalized approach outperformed sham on depression scores, anhedonia, response or remission rates.
studies.why_it_matters: Accelerated, "personalized" TMS protocols are being marketed aggressively and are expensive; this trial suggests the added personalization did not deliver measurable benefit over placebo in this sample.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you have depression that hasn't responded to medication and a clinic is offering an MRI- or EEG-"personalized" five-day brain stimulation package, it's fair to ask what randomized evidence supports that specific protocol, what it costs, and whether standard TMS or other established options were considered first.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For families weighing costly neuromodulation on behalf of an older relative with persistent depression, this is a reminder that a technology sounding more tailored is not automatically more effective — and that negative trials rarely get the marketing budget positive ones do.
studies.caveats: Small sample (51 randomized, 43 completed); single center; short follow-up (4 weeks); the sample was not specific to older adults; several authors report financial ties to neurotechnology and device companies including Brainsway, Magventure, Wave Neuroscience and Hybrid Harmony.

studies.title: Being 'a little' socially isolated may carry real mortality risk — especially for older women
studies.the_study: Researchers followed 965 community-dwelling adults aged 70-90 in the Sydney Memory and Ageing Study for up to 18 years, scoring each person on a seven-item index of social frailty (things like living alone, limited contact, no social roles or support). Over that period 689 participants died. Among women, those classified as socially 'pre-frail' — an early, milder stage of social vulnerability — had a 40% higher risk of death than socially robust women, even after accounting for age, physical and psychological frailty, education, smoking, alcohol and physical health. Among men, a link with full social frailty appeared only among those with less education and disappeared once all health factors were accounted for.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests the earliest signs of thinning social connection — not just full-blown isolation — may be a meaningful health signal in later life, and that the signal shows up differently for women and men and across education levels.
studies.story_angle_primary: If your social world has quietly shrunk — fewer calls, no regular group, a role you've let go — treat that as worth attention rather than something to shrug off. Consider mentioning changes in your social contacts and activities at your next check-up the same way you'd mention a change in appetite or sleep, and look into community groups, volunteering or faith and hobby circles that rebuild routine contact.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For families and senior living staff: standard screening tends to flag people who are already severely isolated. These data suggest keeping an eye on residents and relatives in the 'in-between' zone — still somewhat connected but drifting — and that women with less formal education may warrant particular attention in outreach and programming.
studies.caveats: Observational cohort — cannot establish that social pre-frailty causes earlier death; single Australian cohort of older urban adults, which may not generalize; the men's findings weakened after full adjustment; subgroup analyses by sex and education reduce effective sample sizes.

studies.title: Big trial: pausing arthritis drugs around a COVID booster didn't boost antibodies — but did trigger flares
studies.the_study: The COVER randomized trial enrolled 840 patients with rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis or axial spondyloarthritis (mean age about 60, roughly three-quarters women) who were on stable biologic or JAK inhibitor therapy, and randomly assigned them to either continue their medication or hold it for two weeks after a supplemental COVID-19 vaccine dose. Antibody levels against the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein rose substantially in both groups, with no meaningful difference between them. Holding therapy more than doubled the odds of a disease flare (21% versus 9% reported clinically meaningful worsening), though patients in both arms had recovered by the six-week follow-up.
studies.why_it_matters: Many older adults with inflammatory arthritis have been told — or have assumed — that skipping a dose of their immune-modifying drug will make a vaccine work better; this trial indicates the trade-off is a painful flare for no measurable antibody gain.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you take a biologic or JAK inhibitor for rheumatoid, psoriatic or spine arthritis, ask your rheumatologist whether you really need to hold it around your next COVID vaccine dose — this trial found routine two-week interruptions didn't improve the antibody response and raised your chance of a flare. Don't change your regimen on your own; bring this question to the person who prescribes it.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For caregivers and senior living health staff: vaccination clinics and intake conversations can stop treating drug holds as a default for residents on immunomodulators, and should anticipate increased pain, stiffness and function loss in anyone who does pause therapy — a short-term flare can mean a short-term jump in help needed with dressing, bathing and mobility.
studies.caveats: Measured humoral (antibody) response rather than actual infection or hospitalization outcomes; flare outcomes partly self-reported via questionnaire; wide confidence interval around the primary immunogenicity estimate; pragmatic design with missing data handled by imputation; numerous authors report pharmaceutical industry funding and consulting ties, including from vaccine and arthritis drug makers (AbbVie, Lilly, Novartis, Pfizer, Moderna and others), with NIAMS grant support.

studies.title: Registry analysis of 18,000 men links surgery to better survival in prostate cancer that has spread to lymph nodes
studies.the_study: Investigators used US SEER cancer registry records for 18,287 men diagnosed between 2000 and 2022 with prostate cancer that had reached nearby lymph nodes but not spread to distant organs, and built machine learning models to predict cancer-specific survival. A random survival forest model separated patients into distinct risk groups more accurately than standard statistical approaches. The factor most strongly associated with better survival was having had a radical prostatectomy, followed by lower tumor stage and lower PSA; the team released the model as a web-based calculator.
studies.why_it_matters: Node-positive prostate cancer has long been treated as a gray zone where prognosis varies enormously, and tools that individualize risk could help older men and their doctors weigh aggressive local treatment against watchful or hormone-based approaches.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you or your partner has prostate cancer that has reached nearby lymph nodes, it's reasonable to ask your urologist or oncologist how your individual prognosis is estimated and whether local treatment such as surgery is on the table in your case — but remember this analysis compared men who happened to receive different treatments, so it cannot tell you surgery would be right for you.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For families supporting a man through prostate cancer decisions: risk calculators like this one are increasingly appearing online, and a useful role is helping bring the output into the appointment as a question rather than a conclusion — asking how the man's age, other conditions and tolerance for surgery change the picture.
studies.caveats: Retrospective analysis of registry data — observational, so treatment benefit estimates are vulnerable to selection bias (healthier men are more likely to get surgery) despite statistical weighting; registry data lack detail on comorbidity, hormone therapy and radiation specifics; model performance (C-index around 0.70) is moderate; no prospective validation of the published calculator.

studies.title: Why Some Older Adults Keep Going Back to the ER — and What Makes the Visit Feel Bad
studies.the_study: Researchers in New South Wales, Australia linked hospital and mortality records for 336,283 emergency department presentations by adults aged 65 and older in 2018, following survivors for five years, and paired that with 47,461 patient-reported experience surveys. About 10.6% were 'frequent presenters' with four or more ED visits; multimorbidity, living in rural areas, and living in residential aged care raised the odds, while dementia, osteoporosis, frailty, and non-urgent presentations were linked to lower odds. On the experience side, waits of 60 minutes or more (OR 1.70) and complications (OR 1.63) predicted a negative visit, but by far the strongest predictor was not being given enough information about treatment (OR 5.17).
studies.why_it_matters: Repeat ER use among older adults tracks with unmet complex health and social needs rather than simple medical urgency, and the single biggest driver of a bad ER experience is something fixable — clear communication about what is being done and why.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you or someone with you is in the emergency department, the one thing most strongly tied to a better experience is getting clear information — ask staff directly what the plan is, what the test results mean, and what happens next, and keep asking until you understand. Repeat visits often signal that something in your ongoing care isn't covered, so it's worth raising a pattern of ER trips with your regular doctor.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For aged care operators and family caregivers: residents in aged care and people with multiple chronic conditions were more likely to be frequent ED users, suggesting a role for better after-hours clinical support, advance care planning, and rural care coordination to head off avoidable transfers — and for sending a prepared summary and an advocate with every resident who does go.
studies.caveats: Observational, retrospective design — cannot establish causation; single Australian state, so patterns may not generalize to other health systems; experience outcomes were self-reported and surveys were returned by a subset of patients, raising response bias.

studies.title: Where It Hurts May Predict Where Your Mood Goes Next
studies.the_study: Using the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study, researchers tracked 1,047 adults aged 45 and older who already had depressive symptoms at baseline from 2011 to 2018, mapping how their symptoms changed over seven years. Three paths emerged: mild and stable (13.2%), moderate and worsening (57.5%), and high and persistent (29.4%). Pain at particular body sites predicted the worse paths — finger, wrist, arm, head, and neck pain for the worsening group, and head, arm, neck, toe, and stomach pain for the high-persistent group. Sleep duration explained only a small share (up to about 9%) of these links.
studies.why_it_matters: Persistent pain in specific areas — not just overall pain — appears to travel alongside worsening depression over years, suggesting that treating pain and mood as one package may matter more than treating either alone.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you live with ongoing pain in your hands, arms, neck or head and also feel persistently low, mention both to your doctor in the same visit rather than treating them as separate problems — this study suggests they tend to move together over time.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For caregivers and care staff: routine depression screening for older adults with chronic pain complaints — and vice versa — may catch people on a worsening trajectory earlier, since nearly nine in ten people in this group either worsened or stayed persistently symptomatic.
studies.caveats: Observational cohort — cannot establish causation; pain, sleep, and depressive symptoms were all self-reported; sample limited to Chinese middle-aged and older adults who already had depressive symptoms, so findings may not generalize; mediation analyses were explicitly exploratory.

studies.title: Six Weeks of Squats Improved Balance — Brain Stimulation Added Nothing
studies.the_study: Forty-eight healthy adults were randomized into four groups: squat training with active transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), squat training with sham stimulation, stimulation alone, or sham alone, over six weeks. Balance was measured at baseline, three weeks, six weeks, and one week after the program using standard posturography tests. Both squat training groups significantly improved static and dynamic postural control, including balance with eyes closed, while the brain stimulation added no measurable benefit on top of training — and stimulation alone did not improve balance.
studies.why_it_matters: It reinforces that progressive lower-body strength work is the active ingredient in balance improvement, and offers a caution against paying for add-on neurotechnology that didn't beat sham in a controlled test.
studies.story_angle_primary: If balance is your concern, the evidence here points to the boring thing working: structured, progressive lower-body strength training over about six weeks improved balance, including with eyes closed. Note this trial used heavy barbell squats in healthy adults — ask a physical therapist or trainer to scale a squat-based program safely to your own strength and joint health before starting.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For activity directors and fitness staff in senior living: this is a reminder to invest in supervised, progressive resistance programming rather than novel neuro-stimulation gadgets, which failed to outperform sham here.
studies.caveats: Small N (48 across four groups); participants were healthy adults, not frail or older adults, so results may not generalize to the senior population; short six-week intervention with only one-week follow-up; no falls outcomes measured.

studies.title: Family Doctors Get a Roadmap for Diagnosing and Treating Low Testosterone in Men
studies.the_study: An international panel of general practitioners, endocrinologists, urologists, andrologists and clinical chemists met in Amsterdam in November 2025 and reached unanimous consensus on ten resolutions for managing testosterone deficiency in primary care. Key points: therapy should only start when a man has symptoms or signs plus a low total or free testosterone, with total testosterone under 12 nmol/L (350 ng/dL) considered low; ongoing monitoring of symptoms and bloodwork is essential; and certain complex cases should still be referred to specialists. The panel cited large randomized trial data, including TRAVERSE, indicating testosterone therapy is not associated with increased cardiovascular or prostate cancer risk.
studies.why_it_matters: Low testosterone overlaps heavily with conditions older men already see their GP about — type 2 diabetes, obesity, fatigue, low mood, sexual dysfunction — and this guidance is aimed at getting those men properly evaluated instead of overlooked or sent on long specialist waits.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you're an older man with persistent fatigue, low mood, or sexual difficulties alongside diabetes or obesity, it's reasonable to ask your primary care doctor whether a testosterone check is warranted — but note that these experts say treatment requires both symptoms and a confirmed low blood level, not a lab number alone, plus ongoing monitoring.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For families and care professionals: this is expert consensus, not new trial data, and the sponsoring organization has a stake in the topic — worth knowing when a relative encounters direct-to-consumer testosterone marketing, which frequently skips the symptoms-plus-confirmed-low-level standard the panel insists on.
studies.caveats: This is an expert consensus statement, not original research — no new patient data; sponsored by the Androgen Society, an advocacy organization in this clinical area; several panelists work in men's health clinics and industry-adjacent roles; consensus processes can reflect panel composition as much as evidence.

studies.title: Visual Hallucinations From Sight Loss May Be an Overlooked Cause of Falls
studies.the_study: This clinical review examines Charles Bonnet Syndrome (CBS) — vivid visual hallucinations experienced by people with declining vision, who know the images aren't real. The authors argue that CBS has historically been framed as a psychological issue, but emerging work suggests it also contributes directly to falls, as people react to or navigate around hallucinated images. They note awareness of CBS among both sight loss and falls prevention specialists is low, and call for falls prevention approaches that span primary care, hospital, and community services to account for it.
studies.why_it_matters: Older adults with macular degeneration, glaucoma, or other vision loss who see things that aren't there are often frightened into silence, fearing a dementia diagnosis — naming the condition and linking it to fall risk could change both the conversation and the prevention plan.
studies.story_angle_primary: If your eyesight is failing and you sometimes see patterns, faces, or figures that you know aren't real, that is a recognized condition tied to vision loss — not a sign you are losing your mind. Tell your eye doctor or GP, especially if you've stumbled or startled because of it, because it may belong in your falls prevention plan.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For care staff and families: don't assume reports of visual hallucinations in a resident with sight loss indicate dementia or psychosis — ask about vision status, and consider whether these experiences are contributing to unexplained falls or avoidance of walking.
studies.caveats: This is a narrative clinical review, not original research — no new data, no quantified effect on fall rates; the proposed CBS–falls link rests on an emerging and limited evidence base.

studies.title: A Blood Test for Alzheimer's Sped Up Diagnosis — Without Adding Distress
studies.the_study: Researchers at a memory clinic in Spain randomized 220 new patients (median age 73, 56% women) being evaluated for memory complaints — ranging from subjective cognitive decline to mild dementia — to have blood biomarker results (p-tau217 for Alzheimer's pathology and NfL for nerve damage) shared with them and their neurologist either at 3 months or at 9 months. At the 3-month mark, 50% of the early-disclosure group had a very high-confidence diagnosis versus 4.6% of the delayed group. Early disclosure also led to more Alzheimer's symptomatic treatment started, fewer repeat neuropsychological testing appointments, and more discharges back to primary care — with no increase in anxiety, depression, stress, or reduced quality of life.
studies.why_it_matters: Months of diagnostic uncertainty are among the most difficult parts of a memory workup, and this trial suggests a simple blood draw can shorten that limbo and speed appropriate treatment without the emotional harm many clinicians feared.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you or a partner are being evaluated for memory changes, it's reasonable to ask the memory clinic whether blood-based biomarker testing (p-tau217, NfL) is part of their workup and how soon results would be shared with you — in this trial, getting answers earlier didn't make patients more anxious or depressed.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For families and care coordinators, earlier diagnostic certainty means planning conversations, treatment decisions, and care arrangements can begin months sooner; senior living staff may also see more residents arriving with a confirmed etiologic diagnosis managed by primary care rather than a specialist clinic.
studies.caveats: Single-center trial at one Spanish memory clinic; 9-month follow-up; several authors report consulting and speaking fees from diagnostic and pharmaceutical companies including Roche Diagnostics, Eli Lilly, and Quanterix; emotional outcomes were self-reported; findings may not generalize to health systems with different referral patterns.

studies.title: Calorie Formulas Used in Nursing Homes Are Often Wrong — and Usually Too High
studies.the_study: Brazilian researchers systematically reviewed four studies (total n=332) that compared measured resting metabolic rate — using indirect calorimetry, the gold standard — against the predictive equations routinely used to set calorie targets for residents of long-term care facilities. Nearly four in five equations overestimated energy needs at the group level, and individual accuracy never exceeded 41%. Classic formulas such as Harris-Benedict and FAO/WHO/UNU performed poorly; the Lührmann equation did best, with moderate-quality evidence.
studies.why_it_matters: Calorie prescriptions in long-term care are built on these equations, so systematic overestimation can mean residents are fed more than they need, with downstream metabolic consequences — and no formula should be trusted without ongoing weight and clinical monitoring.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you live in or are moving into a long-term care setting, you can ask how your meal plan's calorie target was calculated and how often your weight and nutritional status are rechecked — a number from a formula is a starting estimate, not a measurement.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Dietitians and nursing home administrators should treat predictive equation outputs as rough estimates requiring clinical follow-up, consider the Lührmann equation over Harris-Benedict, and weigh whether indirect calorimetry is feasible for residents with complex nutritional needs.
studies.caveats: Only four studies with 332 participants total pooled; observational studies only; evidence quality rated moderate at best; institutionalized populations studied may not represent all long-term care residents.

studies.title: Older Adults Keep Their Eyes Glued to the Next Step — and Fall Risk May Show Up in Where They Look
studies.the_study: Researchers systematically reviewed 53 studies that used wearable eye-tracking technology to record where older adults look while walking — during simple walking, walking while distracted, obstacle avoidance, precision stepping, turning, stairs, and navigation. Across studies, older adults fixated more often and for longer on immediately relevant spots like the next foot placement, and spent less time scanning their wider surroundings. Differences in eye-movement timing were mixed overall but most pronounced in older adults at high risk of falls.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests that walking safely takes more visual attention as we age, which helps explain why distraction and cluttered environments raise fall risk — and points toward gaze patterns as a possible future fall-risk marker.
studies.story_angle_primary: Because walking appears to demand more of your visual attention with age, it's worth being deliberate about dividing it — pause before reading your phone, looking at a sign, or turning to talk to someone, and make sure stairs, hallways, and walkways at home are well lit and uncluttered.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For senior living operators and caregivers, this supports environmental design that reduces visual demand — consistent lighting, high-contrast step edges, clear floors — and supports caution about conversing with a resident mid-walk or during stair descent.
studies.caveats: Systematic review of heterogeneous studies using widely varying eye-tracking metrics and walking tasks; observational research that cannot establish that gaze patterns cause falls; no pooled quantitative analysis; generalizability across study populations is limited.

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**
- **Mood and body keep traveling together.** The PREVIOUS digest tied arthritis-heavy multimorbidity to greater depressive burden (PMID 42636431) and traced decades of depressive symptoms into later physical decline (PMID 42633642). The NEW digest sharpens the same thread with **Where It Hurts May Predict Where Your Mood Goes Next (PMID 42749164)**, in which pain at specific sites — hands, arms, neck, head — predicted which older adults' depression worsened over seven years. The practical message in both runs is the same: screen for one when you find the other.
- **Communication, not pharmacology, is the recurring failure point.** The PREVIOUS digest found families in the dark about risperidone's risks in care homes (PMID 42640817). The NEW digest shows the same gap in two more settings: **Sleeping pills stopped in the hospital often come right back home with you (PMID 42785158)**, where a quarter of hospital-achieved sedative reductions unraveled within a year without a follow-up plan, and **Why Some Older Adults Keep Going Back to the ER (PMID 42762629)**, where not being given enough information about treatment was by far the strongest predictor of a bad emergency visit (odds ratio 5.17).
- **Ordinary lab values as prognostic tools.** The PREVIOUS run had the C-reactive protein-to-albumin ratio predicting appendicitis complications (PMID 42634733) and a framework for clinical biological-age panels (PMID 42631826). The NEW run extends this to **A routine blood test may predict survival in people who reach 100 (PMID 42777518)** and **A routine cholesterol number may predict whether ED pills will work for you (PMID 42766789)** — both built from values already sitting in most charts, and both, like their predecessors, honest about only moderate accuracy.

**Advances**
- **Biomarkers moved from "promising" to tested in practice.** The PREVIOUS digest's Mount Sinai framework asked how biological aging measures might enter the clinic (PMID 42631826). The NEW digest supplies an actual randomized answer in the dementia space: **A Blood Test for Alzheimer's Sped Up Diagnosis — Without Adding Distress (PMID 42832237)**, where early disclosure of p-tau217 and NfL results lifted high-confidence diagnosis from 4.6% to 50% at three months with no rise in anxiety or depression.
- **Who qualifies for new Alzheimer's drugs keeps getting more complicated.** The PREVIOUS digest argued frailty should stratify rather than exclude candidates for anti-amyloid therapy (PMID 42641765). The NEW digest adds a second eligibility wrinkle from the opposite direction: **Spinal fluid tests show Alzheimer's-type damage hiding inside Lewy body dementia (PMID 42841041)** suggests a meaningful share of people labeled with Lewy body dementia carry Alzheimer's pathology that may make them candidates for — or at least worth evaluating for — amyloid-targeting treatment.

**Counterpoints**
- The PREVIOUS run leaned optimistic about new measurement and treatment technology reaching older adults. The NEW run supplies a sober correction across three items: **Personalized brain stimulation for stubborn depression fails to beat placebo (PMID 42749167)**, **Six Weeks of Squats Improved Balance — Brain Stimulation Added Nothing (PMID 42753671)**, and **Bed alarms don't prevent falls in hospitals (PMID 42833806)**. Together they argue that adoption in aging care routinely runs ahead of evidence, and that the low-tech comparison arm often wins.

**New themes**
- **Mobility mechanics as a distinct research cluster.** Nothing in the PREVIOUS digest addressed how older people actually walk. The NEW digest has five entries: **A curled toe can rob you of nearly 60% of your push-off power (PMID 42766945)**, **Starting, stopping and turning reveal Parkinson's changes that plain walking misses (PMID 42762698)**, **Older Adults Keep Their Eyes Glued to the Next Step (PMID 42753670)**, **Visual Hallucinations From Sight Loss May Be an Overlooked Cause of Falls (PMID 42833804)**, and the bed alarm review (PMID 42833806).
- **Long-term care operations and financing.** Also new: **How long does Medicaid home care actually last? (PMID 42834564)** and **Calorie Formulas Used in Nursing Homes Are Often Wrong (PMID 42759166)** push into provider and payer territory the PREVIOUS run didn't touch.
- **Social connection graduates from qualitative to mortality data.** The PREVIOUS digest explored television as a "mediated companion" for women living alone (PMID 42634112). The NEW digest's **Being 'a little' socially isolated may carry real mortality risk (PMID 42762630)** puts an 18-year survival number on the milder, earlier stage of that same problem.
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Six studies in this batch quietly rewrite where fall risk actually lives — and what we've been doing about it. **Bed alarms don't prevent falls in hospitals (PMID 42833806)** and **Six Weeks of Squats Improved Balance — Brain Stimulation Added Nothing (PMID 42753671)** show two popular interventions failing, while **A curled toe can rob you of nearly 60% of your push-off power (PMID 42766945)**, **Visual Hallucinations From Sight Loss May Be an Overlooked Cause of Falls (PMID 42833804)**, **Older Adults Keep Their Eyes Glued to the Next Step (PMID 42753670)**, and **Starting, stopping and turning reveal Parkinson's changes that plain walking misses (PMID 42762698)** locate real, checkable risk in the feet, the eyes, and the moments of starting, turning and stopping. The common thread: the alarm on the bed and the gadget in the gym are getting attention that a foot exam, a lighting check and a strength program have earned.

**Why pitch this now:** Falls remain the leading cause of injury and injury death in older adults, hospitals and senior living communities are actively debating whether to pull their alarm systems, and families are being sold balance technology that didn't beat a sham in a controlled test — so the question of what deserves the money and the attention is live right now.

**Angle:** A reported feature that walks a reader through a realistic fall-risk review — toes, vision, lighting, doorways and turns, leg strength, medications — while explaining why the most visible safety measures in hospitals and care communities are the ones with the thinnest evidence. Written for older adults and family caregivers, with a sidebar of questions for senior living administrators and hospital nurse leaders.

**Potential headlines:**
- What Actually Prevents Falls, According to a Year of New Research
- The Bed Alarm Was Never the Answer — Check the Feet and the Lighting Instead
- Six Things Worth Checking Before Your Next Fall

**Potential outlets:**
- **National Council on Aging** — runs the country's best-known falls prevention programming and could turn an evidence-sorting piece like this into practical consumer guidance.
- **Next Avenue** — the "what works versus what gets marketed" framing, grounded in named studies, fits their service-journalism-with-evidence lens for older readers and families.
- **LeadingAge** — the de-implementation argument on alarms is a direct provider and quality-improvement story for nonprofit senior housing and nursing home leadership.
- **Caring.com** — readers are actively choosing communities and home-care arrangements; a checklist of fall-risk questions to ask a provider matches their decision-stage audience.
pitch_ideas_raw:
- **Sleeping pills stopped in the hospital often come right back home with you (PMID 42785158):** The discharge handoff as the weak link in deprescribing — build the piece around a two-week post-discharge medication check-in with a pharmacist, for a caregiver-advice column.
- **How long does Medicaid home care actually last? A decade of data offers an answer (PMID 42834564):** Five-year numbers that counter the assumption home care is a short bridge to the nursing home — a planning explainer for families mapping long-term care finances, and a demand-forecasting brief for senior living trade press.
- **Spinal fluid tests show Alzheimer's-type damage hiding inside Lewy body dementia (PMID 42841041):** "A Lewy body diagnosis may not be the whole story" — what mixed pathology means for prognosis conversations and trial eligibility, for a consumer health explainer or dementia caregiver newsletter.
- **A curled toe can rob you of nearly 60% of your push-off power when you walk (PMID 42766945):** The foot deformity families dismiss as cosmetic may be eroding walking power — pitch as a podiatry-and-mobility piece for a consumer health section, with a staff-training brief for assisted living.
- **A routine cholesterol number may predict whether ED pills will work for you (PMID 42766789):** When an ED medication stops working, treat it as a prompt for a heart and blood sugar check rather than a higher dose — a men's health column.
- **A routine blood test may predict survival in people who reach 100 (PMID 42777518):** A careful explainer on what creatinine-to-cystatin-C can and can't tell you about muscle loss, and why grip strength and protein intake still matter more — consumer health, with an emphasis on not over-reading a lab number.
- **Bed alarms don't prevent falls in hospitals — and experts are now trying to phase them out (PMID 42833806):** Why the most audible safety device in the building may be doing nothing — a senior-living and hospital trade feature on de-implementation as a quality project, plus a short consumer piece on what to ask when an alarm is switched on.
- **Starting, stopping and turning reveal Parkinson's changes that plain walking misses (PMID 42762698):** Coach readers to describe transitions, not "my walking is worse," at the next neurology appointment — a Parkinson's caregiver column, with an environmental-design angle for memory care and assisted living.
- **Personalized brain stimulation for stubborn depression fails to beat placebo in a controlled trial (PMID 42749167):** A consumer-protection piece on expensive five-day "personalized" TMS packages and the questions to ask before paying — consumer health or a money-and-aging section.
- **Being 'a little' socially isolated may carry real mortality risk — especially for older women (PMID 42762630):** The in-between zone — still connected, but drifting — as the group routine screening misses, and why women with less formal education may need targeted outreach; fits a community-programming trade piece or a thoughtful consumer feature on rebuilding routine contact.
- **Big trial: pausing arthritis drugs around a COVID booster didn't boost antibodies — but did trigger flares (PMID 42832241):** Clear, timely vaccine-season guidance for the many older adults on biologics who assume they should hold their dose — a consumer health explainer or local-news health segment, with the "don't change it yourself" caution front and center.
- **Registry analysis of 18,000 men links surgery to better survival in prostate cancer that has spread to lymph nodes (PMID 42690326):** How to bring an online risk calculator into an oncology appointment as a question rather than a verdict — a patient-navigation piece for a cancer or men's health section.
- **Why Some Older Adults Keep Going Back to the ER — and What Makes the Visit Feel Bad (PMID 42762629):** Clear information beat wait times as the driver of a bad emergency visit — a practical "what to ask in the ER" caregiver column, paired with a trade brief on after-hours support and avoidable transfers from residential care.
- **Where It Hurts May Predict Where Your Mood Goes Next (PMID 42749164):** Bring pain and low mood to the same appointment — a chronic pain and mental health explainer for a consumer health section.
- **Six Weeks of Squats Improved Balance — Brain Stimulation Added Nothing (PMID 42753671):** The unglamorous intervention won — a fitness-and-aging piece on scaling squat-based training safely, for a consumer wellness column or senior living activity-director trade brief.
- **Family Doctors Get a Roadmap for Diagnosing and Treating Low Testosterone in Men (PMID 42647144):** Use the panel's own standard — symptoms plus a confirmed low level plus monitoring — as a yardstick against direct-to-consumer testosterone marketing, for a men's health consumer piece that notes the sponsor's stake.
- **Visual Hallucinations From Sight Loss May Be an Overlooked Cause of Falls (PMID 42833804):** "You're not losing your mind" — naming Charles Bonnet Syndrome for people with macular degeneration or glaucoma, and putting it in the falls plan; strong fit for a vision-loss or caregiver-advice column.
- **A Blood Test for Alzheimer's Sped Up Diagnosis — Without Adding Distress (PMID 42832237):** Shortening the months of diagnostic limbo without emotional harm — a consumer explainer on asking memory clinics about p-tau217 and NfL, plus a trade note that more residents may arrive with a confirmed diagnosis managed in primary care.
- **Calorie Formulas Used in Nursing Homes Are Often Wrong — and Usually Too High (PMID 42759166):** A dietitian-facing trade piece on treating equation outputs as estimates and rechecking weight, with a short consumer version on what to ask about a loved one's meal plan.
- **Older Adults Keep Their Eyes Glued to the Next Step (PMID 42753670):** Walking takes more visual attention with age — why reading your phone on the stairs or chatting mid-walk raises risk, and what lighting and contrast changes help; a home-safety consumer piece and an environmental-design brief for operators.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: Senior Living Research Digest — October 2026
**Checked:** 2026-10-07 | **Studies reviewed:** 20
**Primary audience:** older adults and seniors | **Secondary audience:** families, caregivers, and senior living professionals

---

### Study 1: Sleeping pills stopped in the hospital often come right back home with you
**PMID:** 42785158 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 2: How long does Medicaid home care actually last? A decade of data offers an answer
**PMID:** 42834564 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Overstated duration claim** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "these numbers show most older adults who start them use them for years"
- **Abstract says:** "Among older adults with 5 years of follow-up (n = 591), 25.2% ended HCBS with community discharge, 16.2% with nursing home entry, and 26.2% with death. The remaining 32.3% still used HCBS... Extended duration of HCBS use was common across our sample"
- **Problem:** The abstract reports no median duration; only 32.3% of the five-year subgroup were still enrolled at five years, so 'most ... use them for years' is an inference the abstract does not support numerically.
- **Suggested fix:** "Rephrase as 'extended use was common — about a third of those followed five years were still receiving services.'"

**Issue B. 'Norm rather than the exception'** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "know that long enrollments are the norm rather than the exception"
- **Abstract says:** "Extended duration of HCBS use was common across our sample, which may affect Medicaid's ability to fund HCBS programs."
- **Problem:** 'Common' in the abstract is softened language; 'the norm rather than the exception' implies a majority figure the abstract does not provide.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say 'long enrollments were common in this cohort.'"

### Study 3: Spinal fluid tests show Alzheimer's-type damage hiding inside Lewy body dementia
**PMID:** 42841041 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Unquantified prevalence** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "People with DLB frequently showed abnormal amyloid and tau levels"
- **Abstract says:** "Compared to controls, amyloid and tau levels were abnormal in DLB, but not in PD."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports group-level abnormality, not how many individuals were biomarker-positive; 'frequently' and later 'a substantial share' imply a proportion that is not given.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say 'As a group, people with DLB showed abnormal amyloid and tau levels compared with controls (the abstract does not give the share who were positive).'"

**Issue B. Causal wording for cross-sectional association** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "a substantial share of people diagnosed with Lewy body dementia also carry Alzheimer's pathology that is dragging their thinking down"
- **Abstract says:** "Amyloid and tau positivity in DLB were associated with worse global cognitive outcomes, but not with motor performance."
- **Problem:** 'Dragging their thinking down' asserts causation from an association measured in a cross-sectional biomarker comparison.
- **Suggested fix:** "Use 'is associated with worse global cognition.'"

**Issue C. Implied longitudinal decline** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "mixed pathology is common and tracks with faster cognitive decline rather than motor decline"
- **Abstract says:** "Amyloid and tau positivity in DLB were associated with worse global cognitive outcomes, but not with motor performance."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports worse cognitive outcomes at assessment, not a faster rate of decline over time; no longitudinal follow-up is described.
- **Suggested fix:** "Change to 'tracks with worse cognition rather than worse motor function.'"

### Study 4: A curled toe can rob you of nearly 60% of your push-off power when you walk
**PMID:** 42766945 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 5: A routine cholesterol number may predict whether ED pills will work for you
**PMID:** 42766789 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 6: A routine blood test may predict survival in people who reach 100
**PMID:** 42777518 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 7: Bed alarms don't prevent falls in hospitals — and experts are now trying to phase them out
**PMID:** 42833806 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline asserts a conclusion not in the abstract** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Bed alarms don't prevent falls in hospitals — and experts are now trying to phase them out"
- **Abstract says:** "The review covers the evidence for fall prevention alarms and other fall prevention practices, factors that contribute to overuse of fall prevention alarms, and strategies that are being tested to de-implement fall prevention alarms."
- **Problem:** The abstract does not state that alarms fail to prevent falls; it only says the review examines the evidence and de-implementation strategies. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Soften to 'Review questions the evidence behind hospital bed alarms — and looks at how to phase them out.'"

**Issue B. Unsourced harms list** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "they can increase noise, disrupt sleep, add to staff alarm fatigue and discourage patients from moving — while the evidence that they actually prevent falls is thin"
- **Abstract says:** "The review covers the evidence for fall prevention alarms and other fall prevention practices, factors that contribute to overuse... and an overview of low-value care and de-implementation science."
- **Problem:** None of these specific harms, nor the characterization of the evidence as 'thin', appear in the abstract. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Attribute these points to the review's full text or state that the abstract does not detail specific harms."

**Issue C. Alternatives presented as evidence-supported** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Ask instead about the things that do have support: a medication review, mobility assistance, toileting schedules and safe footwear"
- **Abstract says:** "The review covers the evidence for fall prevention alarms and other fall prevention practices..."
- **Problem:** The abstract does not name any specific alternative practices or say which have supporting evidence.
- **Suggested fix:** "Note that the review discusses 'other fall prevention practices' without listing them in the abstract."

### Study 8: Starting, stopping and turning reveal Parkinson's changes that plain walking misses
**PMID:** 42762698 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 9: Personalized brain stimulation for stubborn depression fails to beat placebo in a controlled trial
**PMID:** 42749167 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 10: Being 'a little' socially isolated may carry real mortality risk — especially for older women
**PMID:** 42762630 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 11: Big trial: pausing arthritis drugs around a COVID booster didn't boost antibodies — but did trigger flares
**PMID:** 42832241 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 12: Registry analysis of 18,000 men links surgery to better survival in prostate cancer that has spread to lymph nodes
**PMID:** 42690326 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 13: Why Some Older Adults Keep Going Back to the ER — and What Makes the Visit Feel Bad
**PMID:** 42762629 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 14: Where It Hurts May Predict Where Your Mood Goes Next
**PMID:** 42749164 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Predictive language for associational finding** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Pain at particular body sites predicted the worse paths — finger, wrist, arm, head, and neck pain for the worsening group"
- **Abstract says:** "In fully adjusted models, the strongest associations with the Moderate-Increasing trajectory were observed for finger, wrist, arm, head, and neck pain"
- **Problem:** The multinomial regression tested associations with trajectory membership, not prospective prediction; 'predicted' implies more than the design supports.
- **Suggested fix:** "Change to 'Pain at particular body sites was associated with the worse paths'."

### Study 15: Six Weeks of Squats Improved Balance — Brain Stimulation Added Nothing
**PMID:** 42753671 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Stimulation-alone claim not stated in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "and stimulation alone did not improve balance"
- **Abstract says:** "The sham tDCS + ST group significantly improved in SOT composite scores and US with eyes closed (ECL) compared to the a-tDCS and sham tDCS at T2 and T3, with significant within-group gains from baseline."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports that the training groups outperformed the stimulation-only and sham-only groups, but never states that the a-tDCS-alone group failed to improve from baseline; this is an inference.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say 'the stimulation-only group did not match the training groups' improvements' rather than asserting no improvement."

**Issue B. Participant age not reported in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "participants were healthy adults, not frail or older adults, so results may not generalize to the senior population"
- **Abstract says:** "Forty-eight participants were randomized into four groups ... in healthy adults"
- **Problem:** The abstract describes the sample only as 'healthy adults' and gives no ages, so the assertion that they were not older adults is unverifiable from abstract only (though the generalizability caution itself is reasonable).
- **Suggested fix:** "Reword to 'participants were described only as healthy adults, with no ages reported, so applicability to frail or older people is unknown'."

### Study 16: Family Doctors Get a Roadmap for Diagnosing and Treating Low Testosterone in Men
**PMID:** 42647144 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Panelist conflict characterization unverifiable** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "several panelists work in men's health clinics and industry-adjacent roles"
- **Abstract says:** "An international panel of experts- including GPs, endocrinologists, urologists, andrologists, and clinical chemists- convened in Amsterdam in November 2025 ... International multidisciplinary consensus initiative sponsored by the Androgen Society."
- **Problem:** Affiliations show men's health clinic practice for some panelists, but there is no conflict-of-interest statement in the abstract supporting 'industry-adjacent roles'. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Limit to what is visible in the affiliations ('several panelists practice in men's health clinics') or note that no conflict-of-interest statement accompanies the abstract."

### Study 17: Visual Hallucinations From Sight Loss May Be an Overlooked Cause of Falls
**PMID:** 42833804 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Added mechanism not in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "it also contributes directly to falls, as people react to or navigate around hallucinated images"
- **Abstract says:** "recent work has highlighted that CBS may also lead to physical outcomes by causing and increasing susceptibility to falls"
- **Problem:** The abstract states a causal/susceptibility link but offers no mechanism; the 'react to or navigate around hallucinated images' explanation is the digest's own addition. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Drop the mechanism clause or attribute it explicitly as a plausible explanation not detailed in the abstract."

**Issue B. Unsourced background claim in 'Why it matters'** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "are often frightened into silence, fearing a dementia diagnosis"
- **Abstract says:** "Charles Bonnet Syndrome (CBS) refers to visual hallucinations associated with a decline in vision ... awareness of CBS among sight loss and falls prevention specialists is low"
- **Problem:** Under-reporting due to fear of a dementia label is widely described in the CBS literature but is not stated in this abstract.
- **Suggested fix:** "Attribute to general CBS literature or soften to 'awareness is low among specialists, so the condition is often missed'."

### Study 18: A Blood Test for Alzheimer's Sped Up Diagnosis — Without Adding Distress
**PMID:** 42832237 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 19: Calorie Formulas Used in Nursing Homes Are Often Wrong — and Usually Too High
**PMID:** 42759166 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. 'Pooled' implies meta-analysis** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Only four studies with 332 participants total pooled"
- **Abstract says:** "A systematic review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines and registered in PROSPERO ... Four studies (n == 332) were included."
- **Problem:** The abstract describes a systematic review with QUADAS-2 and GRADE appraisal; no quantitative pooling/meta-analysis is reported.
- **Suggested fix:** "Change to 'Only four studies with 332 participants in total were included, with no quantitative pooling'."

### Study 20: Older Adults Keep Their Eyes Glued to the Next Step — and Fall Risk May Show Up in Where They Look
**PMID:** 42753670 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Specific gaze target added** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "older adults fixated more often and for longer on immediately relevant spots like the next foot placement"
- **Abstract says:** "more and longer fixations at immediately relevant locations and less time engaging in exploratory gaze behaviors"
- **Problem:** The abstract says 'immediately relevant locations' without specifying foot placement; the headline ('Eyes Glued to the Next Step') builds on this added detail.
- **Suggested fix:** "Use 'immediately relevant locations such as the walking path ahead' or drop the specific example and adjust the headline accordingly."

## Issue Summary

| Study # | Headline | Verdict | Notes |
|---------|----------|---------|-------|
| 1 | Sleeping pills stopped in the hospital often come right back home with you | ✅ Accurate | Numbers, design, population and the lone significant predictor all match the abstract; caveats appropriately flag the exploratory single-center retrospective design. |
| 2 | How long does Medicaid home care actually last? A decade of data offers an answer | ⚠️ Minor issues | All reported percentages and the cessation predictors match; the framing that 'most' beneficiaries use HCBS for years goes slightly beyond what the abstract reports. |
| 3 | Spinal fluid tests show Alzheimer's-type damage hiding inside Lewy body dementia | ⚠️ Minor issues | Cohort size, biomarkers, assay platform and group-level findings are correct, but the digest adds unquantified prevalence language and converts a cross-sectional association into causal/longitudinal wording. |
| 4 | A curled toe can rob you of nearly 60% of your push-off power when you walk | ✅ Accurate | Sample sizes, 58.7% push-off power reduction, 41% GRF reduction and the proximal-compensation interpretation all match; caveats correctly note the small cross-sectional design. |
| 5 | A routine cholesterol number may predict whether ED pills will work for you | ✅ Accurate | Response rate, AIP and diabetes odds ratios, AUC and the authors' 'adjunctive marker' caution are all reproduced correctly. |
| 6 | A routine blood test may predict survival in people who reach 100 | ✅ Accurate | Cohort size, formula, 3.7% per-unit figure, cutoffs (59.3/63.1/64.2, rounded) and the 'moderate discrimination, surrogate marker' framing all match. |
| 7 | Bed alarms don't prevent falls in hospitals — and experts are now trying to phase them out | ⚠️ Minor issues | The review's scope is described correctly, but the headline's flat 'don't prevent falls' and the specific harms listed in 'Why it matters' are not stated in this brief abstract. |
| 8 | Starting, stopping and turning reveal Parkinson's changes that plain walking misses | ✅ Accurate | Dataset, sample sizes (91 PD / 78 controls), sensor placement and the steady-state versus complex-task parameter findings match the abstract; caveats correctly disclaim fall predictions. |
| 9 | Personalized brain stimulation for stubborn depression fails to beat placebo in a controlled trial | ✅ Accurate | Randomization (51 randomized, 43 completed), three arms, 10 sessions/day for five days, 1- and 4-week assessments, null primary and secondary outcomes, and the listed industry ties all match the abstract and disclosure statement. |
| 10 | Being 'a little' socially isolated may carry real mortality risk — especially for older women | ✅ Accurate | N, age range, 18-year follow-up, 689 deaths, HR 1.40 for socially pre-frail women, and the education-dependent, adjustment-sensitive male finding are all reported correctly, with non-causal framing. |
| 11 | Big trial: pausing arthritis drugs around a COVID booster didn't boost antibodies — but did trigger flares | ✅ Accurate | N, demographics, GMFR null result, flare OR and questionnaire percentages all match the abstract; industry/NIAMS funding and imputation handling are flagged in Caveats. |
| 12 | Registry analysis of 18,000 men links surgery to better survival in prostate cancer that has spread to lymph nodes | ✅ Accurate | Sample (18,287 N1M0 SEER patients, 2000-2022), RSF outperformance, SHAP ranking (radical prostatectomy > lower T stage > PSA), C-index ~0.70 and the web calculator all match. Caveat about missing comorbidity/hormone/radiation detail is general SEER knowledge not stated in the abstract, but it is appropriately cautionary rather than overstated. |
| 13 | Why Some Older Adults Keep Going Back to the ER — and What Makes the Visit Feel Bad | ✅ Accurate | 336,283 index presentations, 10.6% frequent presenters, 47,461 surveys, and all three odds ratios (1.70, 1.63, 5.17) match. Digest omits a couple of predictors (female sex, hospitalisation, triage below resuscitation) but nothing is misstated. |
| 14 | Where It Hurts May Predict Where Your Mood Goes Next | ⚠️ Minor issues | Trajectory percentages, pain-site lists and the ~9% indirect effect are all correct; only the word 'predicted' slightly overstates an associational analysis, and Caveats already note non-causality. |
| 15 | Six Weeks of Squats Improved Balance — Brain Stimulation Added Nothing | ⚠️ Minor issues | Design, N=48, four arms, assessment timepoints and the null tDCS add-on effect are accurate; two small inferences go slightly past what the abstract states. |
